chapters.tagline: The HRT decision — what to ask for
chapters.title: The HRT Decision

sections.title: What changed, what to ask for, and how to think about it

blocks.label: VALIDATION
blocks.text: If you’ve heard “HRT is dangerous” and you’re terrified, or “HRT is a fountain of youth” and you’re skeptical — that’s real. The conversation around HRT has been a mess for 20+ years. This chapter is here to give you a clear, evidence-informed framework for making your own decision. Let’s start.

sections.title: The short version (if you read nothing else)

items: **HRT is not one thing.** The Women’s Health Initiative studied particular regimens in postmenopausal participants with an average age in the early sixties. Its findings remain important, but risks and benefits vary with age, time since menopause, formulation, route, dose, duration, and individual health.

**For many healthy symptomatic women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset**, the benefit-risk balance of systemic hormone therapy may be favourable after individualized assessment. Evidence does not make one regimen best or safe for everyone.
**HRT is not a fountain of youth.** It does not prevent aging. It does not prevent all chronic disease. It treats symptoms — and for many women, that’s enough.
**HRT is not for everyone.** Some women have medical reasons not to take it. Some women don’t want to. Some women don’t need it. All three are valid.
**The decision should be shared.** Your preferences matter, and a qualified clinician should help assess contraindications, alternatives, follow-up, and changing risks over time.

blocks.text: This chapter gives you the framework to make that decision.

sections.title: Why your doctor might still be cautious

blocks.text: Many doctors were trained during the post-WHI era and were taught that HRT is dangerous. The 2002 study made headlines, prescribing dropped 80% almost overnight, and a generation of clinicians learned “avoid HRT.”

Later analyses and other studies clarified that absolute risks vary by factors such as age and time since menopause. Comparisons between formulations and routes also draw on observational evidence, which cannot answer every question with the certainty of a randomized trial.

So your doctor isn’t being dismissive or ignorant. They’re practicing what they were taught. Your job is to bring them updated information, not to argue. The doctor scripts at the end of this chapter are designed for exactly this.

sections.title: Inside the WHI: two arms, two different stories

blocks.text: The 2002 Women’s Health Initiative had two main arms:

items: **Estrogen + Progestin arm** (for women with a uterus) — used oral conjugated equine estrogen (Premarin) + medroxyprogesterone acetate (Provera). This arm was stopped early because of increased breast cancer and cardiovascular events.

**Estrogen-only arm** (for women without a uterus) — used oral conjugated equine estrogen alone. It did not show the same breast-cancer pattern as the combined-therapy arm. Cardiovascular effects varied by age and timing, and the trial was not a test of today’s many formulations and routes.

blocks.text: The takeaway the media ran with: “HRT causes cancer and heart attacks.”
The takeaway the data actually showed: “This specific combination, in this specific population (women 10+ years past menopause), has risks. Other formulations, in other populations, may not.”
Later analyses and subsequent evidence clarified several points:

items: **Age matters** — women who started HRT in their 50s (within 10 years of menopause) had a different risk profile than women who started in their 70s.
**Route and dose matter** — observational evidence suggests transdermal estrogen may carry a lower clot risk than oral estrogen, but treatment still requires individual risk assessment.
**The progestogen matters** — different agents may have different effects, but direct long-term comparative evidence is more limited than simple “safe versus unsafe” summaries imply.

blocks.alt: A skin patch enters circulation directly, an oral tablet passes through the liver, and local treatment stays near vaginal tissue.

blocks.text: HRT is not one category. The molecule, the route, the dose, and the timing all matter.

rows: The estrogen used in the WHI trials; benefits and risks depend on whether a progestogen is also used and on individual factors.
Body-identical estradiol; oral therapy has more first-pass liver effects than transdermal therapy.
Body-identical estradiol; may be favored when clot or metabolic risk makes avoiding first-pass liver effects important.
Very low dose. For genitourinary symptoms only. Minimal systemic absorption.
Synthetic progestin used with estrogen in the combined WHI arm.
Body-identical progesterone; may have advantages for some patients, but suitability and regimen are individualized.

blocks.title: The framework: Type, Dose, Route, Timing

blocks.text: When discussing HRT with your doctor, ask about all four:

items: **Type** — which estrogen and, if you have a uterus, which endometrial-protective progestogen
**Dose** — the lowest effective dose for the treatment goal
**Route** — oral, transdermal, or local vaginal therapy based on symptoms and risk factors
**Timing** — benefits and risks are generally most favorable for healthy symptomatic women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset, but decisions are individualized

sections.title: Progesterone alone: one possible starting point

blocks.text: For selected women, a clinician may discuss oral micronized progesterone without estrogen. Evidence for sleep or vasomotor symptoms exists but is more limited than the evidence base for standard estrogen-containing menopausal hormone therapy, and it is not a universal treatment for rage or insomnia.
This is a doctor conversation. It’s not a DIY supplement. But it’s often a less intimidating starting point than full HRT, and for some women, it’s enough.
The word “bioidentical” gets used in two different ways:

items: **Regulated bioidentical hormones** — estradiol and progesterone that are molecularly identical to what your body makes. These are FDA-approved, available at standard pharmacies, and have consistent dosing. Examples: Estrace, Prometrium, Climara patch.

**Compounded bioidentical hormones** — custom-mixed by compounding pharmacies, sometimes based on saliva testing. They are not FDA-approved as finished products and do not undergo the same premarket review for safety, effectiveness, and dose consistency as approved products. Compounding still operates under pharmacy regulation and may be medically necessary in limited circumstances, such as a true allergy to an ingredient in available products.

blocks.text: The marketing for compounded bioidenticals often implies they’re “safer” or “more natural” than FDA-approved hormones. There’s no evidence for this. In fact, the lack of quality control means you may be getting more or less than the label says.
**Prefer FDA-approved body-identical products when an appropriate approved option exists.** Discuss any need for compounding with a qualified prescriber.

blocks.label: CAUTION
blocks.text: Systemic HRT may be contraindicated or require specialist assessment in people with:

items: History of breast cancer (especially hormone-receptor-positive)
History of blood clots (DVT, PE)
History of stroke or heart attack
History of endometrial cancer
Active liver disease
Unexplained vaginal bleeding
Pregnancy

blocks.text: **Low-dose vaginal estrogen** has minimal systemic absorption and can be considered separately from systemic HRT. People with a history of estrogen-dependent cancer should make this decision with their oncologist or menopause specialist.

blocks.label: INFORMATION
blocks.text: Bring this script to your appointment:

**“I’ve been experiencing [list your top 2-3 symptoms] for [X months]. I’ve read about the current evidence on HRT — specifically transdermal estradiol and oral micronized progesterone — and I’d like to discuss whether this might be appropriate for me given my medical history and risk factors. If it’s appropriate, what’s the lowest effective dose I could start with? If it’s not appropriate, what are my alternatives?”**
This sentence does four things:

items: It describes your specific symptoms
It shows you’ve done informed research
It asks about your specific situation (not a generic “is HRT safe?”)
It opens the door to alternatives if HRT isn’t right for you

sections.title: If your doctor says “HRT is dangerous”

blocks.label: INFORMATION
blocks.text: See [[Appendix D|doctor-scripts]] for the full script. Short version:

**“I understand the concerns based on the 2002 WHI study. My reading of the more recent reanalysis is that the risks were age-dependent, formulation-dependent, and route-dependent. For a woman my age, with my symptoms, would transdermal estradiol specifically be appropriate? If not, can you help me understand why?”**

This isn’t an argument. It’s an invitation to discuss specifics. If your doctor still won’t engage, consider finding a doctor certified by The Menopause Society (menopause.org) or the British Menopause Society.

HRT is one tool. It’s not the only tool. It’s not always the right tool. But for women with significant perimenopause symptoms who don’t have contraindications, it’s often the most effective tool — and the conversation around it has been so distorted by the WHI fallout that many women who would benefit don’t even consider it.

If you’ve tried the protocols in this book for 30 days and your symptoms are still significantly impacting your life, HRT is a conversation worth having. Not a last resort. Not a “giving up.” Just a conversation, with information, with a clinician who takes you seriously.

*You don’t have to decide about HRT today. You don’t have to decide ever. But you do deserve accurate information to make the decision when you’re ready. This chapter is that information. The decision is yours.*

blocks.label: VALIDATION
blocks.text: If you have 3+ symptoms and you’re trying to figure out how to do all the protocols without going crazy — that’s real. Most women in perimenopause do. This section shows you how to combine them without overwhelm.

sections.title: The rule: one at a time, then add

blocks.text: Don’t start three protocols on Monday. You won’t be able to tell what’s working, you’ll overwhelm yourself, and you’ll quit by Friday.
Instead:

items: Pick the symptom that’s worst right now
Do that chapter’s 7-day plan
Add the 30-day reset on top
Once it’s stable (usually week 3–4), add the next-worst symptom’s protocol
Repeat

blocks.text: Most women can comfortably manage 2–3 protocols at once. Beyond that, you’re adding stress — which worsens every symptom.
**Pattern:** You can’t sleep, and when you can’t sleep, you rage. When you rage, you can’t sleep. A vicious cycle.
**The stack:**
Apply Chapter 1 only. The 90-second removal technique from Chapter 2 is fine for in-the-moment rage, but don’t try to fix the rage frequency yet. Focus on sleep.
Continue Chapter 1. Add Chapter 2’s logging — just track when rage episodes happen, intensity, time of day. Don’t add rage interventions yet. You’re collecting data.
By now your sleep should be improving. Add the blood sugar protocol from Chapter 1 (which is the same as Chapter 2’s and Chapter 3’s). This single protocol helps both sleep AND rage.
Add 2–3 resistance training sessions per week. This helps insulin sensitivity (which helps both sleep and rage) and gives you a physical outlet for accumulated tension.
**Expected timeline:** Sleep improves week 1–2. Rage frequency starts dropping week 3–4. By week 8, both should be significantly better.

sections.title: Composite case 2: The Weight-Fatigue-Thyroid Overlap (Chapter 3 + Lab Workup)

blocks.text: **Pattern:** You’re gaining weight, exhausted all the time, cold, with brittle nails. The weight won’t budge despite “doing everything right.”
**The stack:**

This deserves a clinical review rather than a large self-ordered panel. Depending on your history, a clinician may consider a CBC, ferritin or iron studies, TSH, B12, or other targeted tests. You can still use low-risk basics such as regular meals, a consistent sleep schedule, and symptom tracking while you wait, unless a clinician advises otherwise.

items: **If thyroid is off:** Follow your doctor’s treatment plan. This is the priority.
**If ferritin is low:** Start iron repletion (Chapter 5).
**If B12/D is low:** Supplement.
**If labs are normal:** Start Chapter 3’s blood sugar protocol.

blocks.text: Once labs are addressed, add the cortisol rhythm reset from Chapter 7: morning sunlight, delayed caffeine, protein breakfast, NSDR.
Add 2–3 resistance training sessions. This builds muscle (which improves insulin sensitivity), supports thyroid function, and improves energy.
**Expected timeline:** If thyroid is the issue, you’ll feel better within 2–4 weeks of starting medication. If it’s not thyroid, the combined protocol takes 6–8 weeks to show clear results.

sections.title: Composite case 3: The Hair Loss–Iron Depletion Timeline (Chapters 5 & 10)

blocks.text: **Pattern:** You’re losing hair AND having heavy periods. The hair loss started a few months after the heavy periods started.
**The stack:**
Heavy bleeding is the upstream cause. The hair loss is downstream (iron depletion from blood loss). You can’t fix the hair without fixing the bleeding.

Follow Chapter 10’s safety gate. If bleeding is severe (soaking pads in 1 hour), get medical help immediately. If not, start tracking and schedule a doctor’s appointment to discuss options (tranexamic acid, hormonal IUD).
Once bleeding is being addressed, start iron repletion. Use iron bisglycinate (better absorbed, gentler on gut). Take with vitamin C, away from coffee/tea/calcium.
Continue clinician-directed iron repletion when deficiency has been confirmed. Add gentle hair care, and discuss topical minoxidil if the pattern suggests follicle miniaturization.
Hair regrowth takes months. Follow the testing interval and treatment target set by your clinician; there is no single ferritin target that is appropriate for every reader.
**Expected timeline:** Bleeding should improve within 1–2 cycles of treatment. Ferritin should rise over 2–3 months. Visible hair regrowth at 4–6 months.

blocks.alt: Check warning signs first, then choose one priority symptom while recording the others for later review.

blocks.text: If sleep is broken, fix it first. Every other protocol is less effective when you’re sleep-deprived.
Blood sugar affects mood, energy, weight, sleep, and inflammation. It’s the highest-leverage intervention after sleep.
Don’t add supplements speculatively. Get labs first. You can’t fix what you haven’t measured.

blocks.title: 4. One new supplement at a time

blocks.text: If you start three supplements on Monday and feel weird on Wednesday, you won’t know which one caused it. Start one, give it 2 weeks, then add the next.
Keep a simple log: what you started, when, and any changes in symptoms. Without this, you’re guessing.

blocks.title: 6. If you add a medication, don’t add new supplements at the same time

blocks.text: Let your body adjust to the medication first. Then add supplements one at a time, watching for interactions. See [[Appendix B|supplement-matrix]] for the supplement interaction matrix.

The goal isn’t to be on 12 supplements and 4 medications. The goal is to be on the minimum effective dose of the fewest possible interventions. Most women in perimenopause need 2–4 interventions, not 12.

If you’re doing 4+ protocols and feel worse, not better — stop. You’ve crossed the line from “stacking interventions” to “overwhelming your system.” Drop back to 2 protocols (sleep + blood sugar), stabilize, and add slowly.
Brain fog and overwhelm are perimenopause symptoms. The last thing you need is a protocol that adds to them.
*You don’t have to fix everything at once. You don’t have to fix everything ever. Pick what’s worst, fix that, and see how you feel. The rest can wait.*

blocks.text: Bring a short symptom timeline and ask: “Which conditions could mimic or worsen these symptoms, and which tests—if any—fit my history? If a result is borderline, how will we interpret or follow it?”
If you need menopause-specific care, consider a clinician certified by The Menopause Society or an appropriate local menopause service.

Coverage depends on your plan, symptoms, diagnosis codes, and medical necessity. Ask the ordering clinic and laboratory for an estimate before testing. Avoid ordering large direct-to-consumer panels without clinical guidance; abnormal or borderline results can lead to unnecessary cost and confusion.

*You don’t need every lab in this table. You need the ones that match your symptoms. Bring this appendix to your doctor, ask for the specific tests that match your pattern, and ask for the actual numbers — not just “normal” or “abnormal.”*

items: **All prescription medications you take** (including birth control, thyroid meds, antidepressants, blood pressure meds)

blocks.text: Ask: “Are there any interactions I should be aware of between these?”

*Supplements aren’t automatically safe just because they’re “natural.” Some interact dangerously with prescription medications. When in doubt, ask your pharmacist — they’re the experts in drug interactions, and they’re usually free to consult.*

chapters.title: Appendix B2 · How to Read a Supplement Label
chapters.fullTitle: Appendix B2 · How to Read a Supplement Label

sections.title: What the front of the bottle doesn’t tell you

blocks.label: INFORMATION
blocks.text: The supplement industry is largely unregulated. What’s on the front of the bottle is marketing. What’s on the back is what actually matters. This appendix teaches you how to read the back — and what to look for.

sections.title: 1. Look for third-party testing, not just the FDA

blocks.text: The FDA does not regulate supplements the way it regulates medications. Supplement companies are responsible for their own testing, and the FDA only steps in after reports of harm.
What to look for instead:

items: **USP Verified** — United States Pharmacopeia. Independent testing for purity, potency, and contamination.
**NSF Certified for Sport** — National Sanitation Foundation. Stricter than USP, tests for banned substances.
**ConsumerLab.com Verified** — Independent lab that tests supplements for label accuracy.
**UL Verified** — Underwriters Laboratories. Tests for contaminants and label accuracy.

blocks.text: If a supplement doesn’t have at least one of these seals, you’re trusting the manufacturer’s word. Sometimes that’s fine. Often it isn’t.

sections.title: 2. Elemental dose vs. compound weight — the single most common label confusion

blocks.text: This is the trick that gets most people.

**Example:** In a US Supplement Facts panel, “Magnesium 200 mg (as magnesium glycinate)” normally means the serving provides 200 mg of elemental magnesium; “as magnesium glycinate” identifies the compound supplying it. A large number on the front label may instead describe a compound or blend, so use the Supplement Facts panel and serving size—not the front-label headline—to compare products.

Do not multiply a label dose by a universal “absorption percentage” to calculate “usable magnesium.” Absorption varies with the compound, dose, food, the individual, and study method; a fixed percentage creates false precision.

**What to look for:** Check the elemental amount, compound, serving size, other ingredients, and warnings. Magnesium oxide is often more laxative and may be less bioavailable than some other forms, but the best choice depends on why you are taking it, the dose, kidney function, and your medicines. See [[Appendix B|supplement-matrix]] and confirm the choice with your clinician or pharmacist.

sections.title: 3. Why the same mineral in a different form isn’t interchangeable

blocks.text: Magnesium products use different compounds, which can differ in elemental-magnesium content, absorption, tolerability, evidence, and laxative effect:

items: **Magnesium oxide** — supplies magnesium and commonly has a laxative effect; gastrointestinal side effects can limit use.
**Magnesium glycinate** — often marketed as gentler, but product quality and evidence for symptom-specific benefits vary.
**Magnesium citrate** — can have a laxative effect and is also used in some constipation products.

blocks.text: The same applies to:

items: **Iron** — bisglycinate vs. sulfate vs. fumarate (see [[Appendix B|supplement-matrix]])
**Zinc** — picolinate vs. citrate vs. oxide
**Selenium** — methionine vs. selenite
**Chromium** — picolinate vs. GTF vs. polynicotinate

blocks.text: **Check the compound, elemental amount, serving size, other ingredients, and warnings—not just the front-label mineral name.** Ask a pharmacist or clinician which product, if any, fits your medicines, kidney function, pregnancy status, and reason for use.

sections.title: 4. “Proprietary blend” is a red flag for every protocol in this book

blocks.text: If the Supplement Facts panel says “Proprietary Blend” followed by a list of ingredients and a total weight (e.g., “Proprietary Blend: Magnesium, Zinc, B6, B12 … 500mg”), **do not buy this product.**

“Proprietary blend” means the manufacturer doesn’t have to tell you how much of each ingredient is in there. They could put 499mg of the cheapest ingredient and 1mg of the expensive one. You have no way to know.
For any protocol in this book, you need to know the exact dose of each ingredient. **Avoid proprietary blends. Always.**
Before buying any supplement, check the back label for:

items: **Specific form named** (e.g., “magnesium glycinate,” not just “magnesium”)
**Elemental dose specified** (e.g., “Magnesium (as magnesium glycinate) 200mg”)
**No “proprietary blend”** anywhere on the label
**Third-party testing seal** (USP, NSF, ConsumerLab, or UL)
**Expiration date** listed
**Lot number** listed (allows for recall tracking)
**Contact information** for the manufacturer
**No fillers you react to** (common ones: soy, dairy, gluten, artificial colors)

blocks.text: If all 8 boxes are checked, the supplement is likely high-quality. If 3+ are unchecked, find a different brand.
*Supplement quality varies wildly. The same word on the front of the bottle can mean very different things on the back. Learn to read the back — it’s the only part that matters.*

chapters.title: Appendix D · If Your Doctor Says X, You Say Y
chapters.fullTitle: Appendix D · If Your Doctor Says X, You Say Y

blocks.label: INFORMATION
blocks.text: Most women in perimenopause have at least one experience of being dismissed by a healthcare provider. The most common dismissals are predictable — and there are specific, evidence-informed responses to each.
This appendix gives you the exact words. Use them. They’re not aggressive. They’re informed. They shift the conversation from “is this real?” to “what do we do about it?”

sections.title: Scenario 9: “I recommend a compounded bioidentical blend based on your saliva test.”

blocks.text: **If the doctor insists on compounded:** Get a second opinion. Compounded hormones are sometimes appropriate, but they’re often over-prescribed for profit rather than medical need.
Don’t rely on memory. Bring a one-page summary: your top 3 symptoms, when they started, what you’ve tried, what labs you’ve had, what you’re asking for.

blocks.title: 2. Bring a support person if possible

blocks.text: A friend, partner, or family member who can take notes and advocate for you. Especially helpful if you’re dealing with brain fog.
“I’d like to make this decision together, based on the evidence. Can you walk me through your reasoning, and I’ll share mine?”

blocks.title: 4. It’s okay to ask for time

blocks.text: “I’d like to think about this before deciding. Can I follow up next week?”

blocks.title: 5. It’s okay to get a second opinion

blocks.text: Any doctor who gets offended by a second opinion is a doctor to leave. Good doctors welcome second opinions.
After the appointment, write down what was said, what was decided, what labs were ordered. This protects you if there’s ever a question about what was discussed.
*You deserve to be heard. You deserve to be informed. You deserve a doctor who treats you as a partner, not a problem. If your doctor won’t do that, find one who will. They exist.*
